title: Sealing stitch
subtitle: How to work a securing stitch that locks a thread end in place on the back.
excerpt: A sealing stitch (sometimes called a securing stitch) locks a thread end on the back by passing the needle under one existing stitch and then back through the loop it forms. It is a reliable alternative to the run-under method when the surrounding stitches are sparse.
sourceNotes:
Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. Thread ending and securing techniques.
Weldon's Practical Needlework, volume 1 (1886), Internet Archive. Thread securing methods.

glossaryTerms.definition: A self-locking stitch worked by passing the needle under an existing stitch on the back and then back through the loop formed, creating a tight knot-like hold without a true knot.

content.text: is used when the run-under method is not available, for example when ending thread in an area with only one or two stitches nearby. It creates a self-locking hold by threading back through the loop of its own pass.
End the last stitch and bring the needle to the back.
Slide the needle under a nearby existing stitch on the back without catching the cloth.
Pull through slowly, leaving a small loop of thread.
Pass the needle back through the loop before pulling the thread fully taut.
Pull firm. The loop closes around the needle passage and locks the thread end.
Trim the tail flush with the surface of the back.

items.symptom: The lock doesn't hold and the thread pulls free
items.cause: The needle passed through the loop before the loop was properly formed.
items.fix: Leave a loose loop before passing through it. The needle must pass through the circular loop, not through the tail end.

items.symptom: The stitch pulls the nearby stitches out of position
items.cause: The nearby stitch under which the needle was passed was too small or delicate.
items.fix: Choose a larger, more robust nearby stitch to anchor under, or work two sealing stitches in different directions.

content.text: The sealing stitch is useful in all sparse areas of needlework where the run-under method is impractical.
is also used in Sashiko to end a long running-stitch line without disturbing the pattern spacing.
